title: Experimental Chemistry II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 100L introductory chemistry practical curriculum, second semester: systematic qualitative inorganic analysis (cations and anions), gravimetric analysis, redox and complexometric titrations, pH/indicators, and basic organic laboratory techniques such as extraction and simple functional group tests. Deliberately builds beyond CHM107's basic apparatus/volumetric-analysis foundation into systematic analytical schemes.

questions.question: In systematic qualitative inorganic analysis, dilute hydrochloric acid is added first to a solution to test for which group of cations?
options: Group I cations (e.g. Ag+, Pb2+) that form insoluble chlorides
Group II cations that form insoluble sulfides in acidic medium
Alkali metal cations
All cations regardless of group
questions.correct_answer: Group I cations (e.g. Ag+, Pb2+) that form insoluble chlorides
questions.explanation: Dilute HCl precipitates Group I cations such as Ag+, Pb2+, and Hg2^2+ as insoluble white chlorides, the first step in the classical qualitative analysis scheme.

questions.question: A white precipitate forms when dilute HCl is added to a solution, and the precipitate dissolves in hot water. Which cation is most likely present?
options: Pb2+
Ag+
Ba2+
questions.correct_answer: Pb2+
questions.explanation: Lead(II) chloride is unusual among the Group I chlorides in being appreciably soluble in hot water, allowing it to be distinguished from AgCl and Hg2Cl2, which remain insoluble.

questions.question: Which reagent is commonly used to confirm the presence of the carbonate ion (CO3^2-) in a qualitative anion test?
options: Dilute acid, producing effervescence that turns limewater milky
Barium chloride solution only, with no further test needed
Concentrated sulfuric acid producing a brown ring
Silver nitrate producing a yellow precipitate
questions.correct_answer: Dilute acid, producing effervescence that turns limewater milky
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with dilute acid to release CO2 gas, which turns limewater milky/cloudy, confirming the carbonate ion.

questions.question: The addition of acidified barium chloride solution to a solution produces a dense white precipitate insoluble in excess dilute hydrochloric acid. Which anion is indicated?
options: Sulfate (SO4^2-)
Sulfite (SO3^2-)
Carbonate (CO3^2-)
Chloride (Cl-)
questions.correct_answer: Sulfate (SO4^2-)
questions.explanation: Barium sulfate is insoluble even in dilute hydrochloric acid, distinguishing sulfate from sulfite and carbonate, whose barium salts dissolve in dilute acid.

questions.question: Silver nitrate solution is added to a solution containing halide ions. A curdy yellow precipitate insoluble in excess ammonia forms. Which halide is present?
options: Iodide
Chloride
Fluoride
Bromide
questions.correct_answer: Iodide
questions.explanation: Silver iodide is a yellow precipitate that is insoluble even in concentrated ammonia, unlike AgCl (white, dissolves in dilute ammonia) and AgBr (pale yellow, dissolves only in concentrated ammonia).

questions.question: What is the purpose of a flame test in qualitative inorganic analysis?
options: To identify certain metal ions by the characteristic colour they impart to a flame
To determine the melting point of a solid sample
To measure the pH of a solution
To test for the presence of water of crystallization
questions.correct_answer: To identify certain metal ions by the characteristic colour they impart to a flame
questions.explanation: Metal ions such as Na+ (yellow), K+ (lilac), and Ca2+ (brick-red) emit characteristic flame colours due to electron transitions, allowing quick preliminary identification.

questions.question: A sodium salt gives a persistent bright yellow flame in a flame test. What could interfere with correctly identifying a second, less prominent metal ion present in the same sample?
options: The intense sodium flame colour can mask the weaker colours of other ions present
Sodium ions are colourless in a flame and cause no interference
The presence of sodium always prevents any flame test from working
Flame tests cannot detect more than one metal at once under any circumstances
questions.correct_answer: The intense sodium flame colour can mask the weaker colours of other ions present
questions.explanation: Sodium contamination is extremely common and its flame colour is very intense, often masking the presence of other metal ions; a cobalt blue glass filter is sometimes used to screen it out.

questions.question: In gravimetric analysis, what is the main principle used to determine the amount of an analyte in a sample?
options: The analyte is converted to a pure, insoluble compound of known composition, which is then weighed
The analyte's colour intensity is compared to a standard chart
The volume of titrant needed to neutralize the analyte is measured
The analyte's boiling point is measured and compared to a table
questions.correct_answer: The analyte is converted to a pure, insoluble compound of known composition, which is then weighed
questions.explanation: Gravimetric analysis relies on precipitating the analyte as an insoluble compound of known, fixed stoichiometry, then filtering, drying, and weighing it to calculate the original amount.

questions.question: Why must a precipitate in gravimetric analysis be washed with a dilute solution of an appropriate electrolyte rather than pure water alone?
options: Pure water can cause peptization, causing some of the precipitate to pass through the filter
Pure water reacts chemically with the precipitate
Electrolyte solutions dry faster than water
Washing is not necessary if filtration is done quickly
questions.correct_answer: Pure water can cause peptization, causing some of the precipitate to pass through the filter
questions.explanation: Some precipitates can peptize (redisperse into colloidal particles) when washed with pure water, leading to losses through the filter paper; a dilute electrolyte wash solution prevents this.

questions.question: Which type of titration uses a change in colour due to a redox indicator (or the reagent's own colour) to detect the endpoint, such as titrating iron(II) with potassium permanganate?
options: Redox titration
Acid-base titration
Complexometric titration
Precipitation titration
questions.correct_answer: Redox titration
questions.explanation: In redox titrations, an oxidizing or reducing titrant reacts with the analyte via electron transfer; potassium permanganate is self-indicating because it is intensely purple and becomes colourless when reduced.

questions.question: In the titration of acidified iron(II) sulfate solution with potassium permanganate solution, how is the endpoint recognized?
options: The first permanent faint pink colour that persists in the solution
The solution suddenly turns completely colourless
A white precipitate forms
The solution boils vigorously
questions.correct_answer: The first permanent faint pink colour that persists in the solution
questions.explanation: Potassium permanganate is self-indicating; while Fe2+ remains to be oxidized the purple colour is discharged, and the endpoint is reached when a faint pink colour persists, showing excess unreacted permanganate.

questions.question: Why must permanganate titrations involving iron(II) be carried out in an acidic (usually dilute sulfuric acid) medium rather than neutral or basic conditions?
options: Acidic conditions ensure permanganate is reduced fully to Mn2+, giving a predictable, quantitative reaction
Basic conditions destroy the iron(II) ions before titration begins
Acid is only needed to dissolve the iron(II) sulfate
Permanganate does not dissolve in neutral solutions
questions.correct_answer: Acidic conditions ensure permanganate is reduced fully to Mn2+, giving a predictable, quantitative reaction
questions.explanation: In acidic medium, MnO4- is reduced cleanly to Mn2+ (colourless), giving a well-defined 1-electron-per-Fe2+ stoichiometry; in neutral or basic medium it is reduced instead to brown MnO2, complicating the reaction.

questions.question: What is the purpose of adding an indicator such as Eriochrome Black T in a complexometric titration of Ca2+/Mg2+ with EDTA?
options: To signal the endpoint by changing colour when free metal ions are fully complexed by EDTA
To adjust the pH of the solution
To act as the titrant itself
To precipitate the metal ions before titration
questions.correct_answer: To signal the endpoint by changing colour when free metal ions are fully complexed by EDTA
questions.explanation: Eriochrome Black T forms a coloured complex with free metal ions; as EDTA is added and complexes all the free metal ions, the indicator is released in its free form, giving a distinct colour change at the endpoint.

questions.question: EDTA titrations used to determine water hardness are an example of which type of titration?
options: Complexometric titration
Acid-base titration
Redox titration
Gravimetric analysis
questions.correct_answer: Complexometric titration
questions.explanation: EDTA forms stable 1:1 chelate complexes with metal ions such as Ca2+ and Mg2+, making it the standard reagent for complexometric determination of water hardness.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct definition of pH?
options: The negative logarithm (base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration
The positive logarithm of the hydroxide ion concentration
The ratio of acid to base in a solution
The temperature at which a solution boils
questions.correct_answer: The negative logarithm (base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration
questions.explanation: pH is defined as pH = -log10[H+], a scale used to express the acidity or alkalinity of a solution.

questions.question: Which instrument gives a direct, precise numerical reading of the pH of a solution, more accurate than an indicator alone?
options: pH meter
Hydrometer
Barometer
Refractometer
questions.correct_answer: pH meter
questions.explanation: A pH meter uses a glass electrode to measure the hydrogen ion activity electrochemically and displays a precise numerical pH value.

questions.question: What is a buffer solution?
options: A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
A solution that has a pH of exactly 7 at all times
Any solution containing only strong acid
A solution used only to clean glassware
questions.correct_answer: A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
questions.explanation: A buffer, typically made from a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and its conjugate acid), maintains a relatively stable pH against small additions of acid or base.

questions.question: Which basic organic technique is used to separate two immiscible liquids, such as an organic product from an aqueous layer, using a separating funnel?
options: Liquid-liquid extraction
Sublimation
Simple distillation
Filtration
questions.correct_answer: Liquid-liquid extraction
questions.explanation: Liquid-liquid extraction uses a separating funnel to partition a solute between two immiscible solvents based on differing solubility, allowing the organic layer to be separated from the aqueous layer.

questions.question: In a simple test-tube reaction, addition of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (Brady's reagent) produces an orange-yellow precipitate. What functional group does this confirm?
options: Carbonyl group (aldehyde or ketone)
Hydroxyl group (alcohol)
Carboxylic acid group
Amine group
questions.correct_answer: Carbonyl group (aldehyde or ketone)
questions.explanation: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine reacts with the carbonyl carbon of aldehydes and ketones to form an orange-yellow hydrazone precipitate, a classic confirmatory test for the carbonyl group.

questions.question: Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with an aldehyde but not with a ketone. What property of aldehydes explains this positive test?
options: Aldehydes are easily oxidized, reducing the silver(I) ammine complex to metallic silver
Aldehydes are more acidic than ketones
Aldehydes have a lower boiling point than ketones
Aldehydes are insoluble in water while ketones are soluble
questions.correct_answer: Aldehydes are easily oxidized, reducing the silver(I) ammine complex to metallic silver
questions.explanation: Aldehydes are readily oxidized to carboxylic acids, and in doing so reduce the diamminesilver(I) complex ion to metallic silver, which deposits as a mirror on the test tube; ketones lack this easily oxidizable hydrogen and do not react.

questions.question: Which test is used to distinguish a carboxylic acid from other organic compounds by observing effervescence?
options: Addition of sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) solution, which produces CO2 gas bubbles
Addition of Tollens' reagent, giving a silver mirror
Addition of Brady's reagent, giving an orange precipitate
Addition of iodine solution, giving a blue-black colour
questions.correct_answer: Addition of sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) solution, which produces CO2 gas bubbles
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are acidic enough to react with sodium bicarbonate to liberate carbon dioxide gas, seen as effervescence, a simple confirmatory test.

questions.question: The iodine-starch test is commonly used to detect which substance?
options: Starch, indicated by a deep blue-black colour with iodine
Glucose, indicated by a red precipitate
Protein, indicated by a purple colour
Fat, indicated by a translucent stain on paper
questions.correct_answer: Starch, indicated by a deep blue-black colour with iodine
questions.explanation: Iodine forms an intensely blue-black coloured complex with the helical structure of starch (amylose), a classic and highly sensitive confirmatory test.

questions.question: Benedict's test is used to detect the presence of which class of compounds, indicated by a colour change from blue to brick-red precipitate on heating?
options: Reducing sugars
Proteins
Fats and oils
Alcohols
questions.correct_answer: Reducing sugars
questions.explanation: Reducing sugars such as glucose reduce the blue copper(II) ions in Benedict's reagent to a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide on heating.

questions.question: During recrystallization, why is it important to use the minimum volume of hot solvent needed to just dissolve the solid?
options: Using excess solvent reduces the yield of crystals recovered on cooling because more solute stays dissolved
Excess solvent will react with the solid
Excess solvent raises the boiling point uncontrollably
It has no effect on yield, only on speed
questions.correct_answer: Using excess solvent reduces the yield of crystals recovered on cooling because more solute stays dissolved
questions.explanation: The amount of solid that stays dissolved in the mother liquor after cooling depends on the volume of solvent used; more solvent means more product remains in solution and is lost, reducing yield.

questions.question: In a systematic scheme of qualitative analysis, hydrogen sulfide gas is passed into an acidified solution to precipitate which group of cations?
options: Group II cations (e.g. Cu2+, Pb2+, As3+) that form insoluble sulfides in acidic medium
Group I cations that form insoluble chlorides
Alkali metals only
All anions present in the solution
questions.correct_answer: Group II cations (e.g. Cu2+, Pb2+, As3+) that form insoluble sulfides in acidic medium
questions.explanation: In the classical qualitative analysis scheme, Group II cations form characteristically insoluble, often coloured sulfides when H2S is passed into an acidified solution, separating them from later groups.

questions.question: A deep blue solution forms when excess ammonia solution is added to a solution suspected of containing copper(II) ions. What confirms the presence of Cu2+?
options: Formation of the deep blue tetraamminecopper(II) complex ion
Formation of a white precipitate
Formation of a yellow precipitate
No colour change at all
questions.correct_answer: Formation of the deep blue tetraamminecopper(II) complex ion
questions.explanation: Excess ammonia reacts with Cu2+ to form the characteristic deep blue [Cu(NH3)4]2+ complex ion, a standard confirmatory test for copper(II).

questions.question: A student determines the percentage of water of crystallization in hydrated copper(II) sulfate (CuSO4.5H2O) by heating a weighed sample to constant mass. What does 'heating to constant mass' mean?
options: Continuing to heat and reweigh until the mass no longer changes between successive weighings
Heating for exactly one hour regardless of mass change
Heating until the sample turns black
Weighing the sample only once after a fixed heating time
questions.correct_answer: Continuing to heat and reweigh until the mass no longer changes between successive weighings
questions.explanation: Heating to constant mass ensures that all the water of crystallization (or other volatile component) has been driven off, confirmed when repeated heating and weighing produce no further mass loss.

questions.question: In back titration, why is a known excess of one reagent added and then titrated against a second standard reagent?
options: It allows determination of substances that react too slowly or incompletely for direct titration
It is always faster than a direct titration
It removes the need for any indicator
It only works for gases, not solids or liquids
questions.correct_answer: It allows determination of substances that react too slowly or incompletely for direct titration
questions.explanation: Back titration is useful when the analyte reacts slowly, is impure, or has no suitable direct indicator; a known excess of reagent is added to react completely, and the unreacted excess is then titrated to determine how much reacted with the analyte.

questions.question: Which colour change would be observed for methyl orange indicator at the endpoint of a strong acid-strong base titration when added to the acid side (going from acid to base)?
options: Red to yellow
Blue to red
Colourless to pink
Yellow to blue
questions.correct_answer: Red to yellow
questions.explanation: Methyl orange is red in acidic solution and turns yellow as the solution becomes more basic, changing colour around pH 3.1-4.4.

questions.question: What is the main hazard associated with concentrated ammonia solution that requires it to be handled in a fume cupboard?
options: It releases pungent, irritating vapour that can harm the respiratory system
It is highly explosive on contact with air
It is radioactive
It is completely odourless and undetectable
questions.correct_answer: It releases pungent, irritating vapour that can harm the respiratory system
questions.explanation: Concentrated ammonia releases significant amounts of irritating, corrosive vapour, so it should be handled in a well-ventilated fume cupboard to protect the respiratory system and eyes.

questions.question: Why is it important to add a few anti-bumping granules when heating a liquid to boiling during distillation?
options: To promote smooth, even boiling and prevent sudden violent bursts of vapour (bumping)
To increase the boiling point of the liquid
To act as a drying agent
To colour the liquid for easier observation
questions.correct_answer: To promote smooth, even boiling and prevent sudden violent bursts of vapour (bumping)
questions.explanation: Anti-bumping granules provide nucleation sites for bubble formation, ensuring smooth, controlled boiling instead of dangerous sudden bumping that can eject hot liquid.
